text.en: Asha drops a ball and it bounces. She asks, why does it bounce? Asking such questions is how science begins. In this chapter we learn how scientists think and work.

Science is a way of finding out how the world works by asking questions, observing, testing and thinking. Science is not only in laboratories. It is in the kitchen, the garden, the playground and the sky. People across India and the world have studied nature for thousands of years, and each generation adds new knowledge.
Curiosity means wanting to know. A curious mind asks what, how and why. A good question can be tested. Why does this plant grow towards the window is a good question to investigate.
Scientists follow steps: observe, ask a question, make a guess called a hypothesis, test it by an experiment, record results and draw a conclusion. An experiment must be fair. We change only one thing at a time and keep the rest the same. Results should be recorded honestly even if they surprise us. Repeating an experiment helps to be sure.
Science helps us make medicines, grow more food, build bridges and send rockets to space. Science also asks us to be careful: always follow safety rules and respect living things and the environment.
Science is a way of finding out how the world works by asking questions, observing, testing and thinking.

board.text: Science and our lives

text.en: Science also asks us to be careful: always follow safety rules and respect living things and the environment.
Asha sees a ball bounce after she drops it. That is an observation. Her idea that a hard surface might make it bounce higher is an explanation to investigate.

board.text: Observation: the ball bounced
Idea to test: the surface matters

text.en: Turn the idea into a question we can investigate. Does the same ball bounce higher from a hard floor or from a soft mat when we release it from the same height?

board.text: Compare the same ball on two surfaces

text.en: Asha predicts that it will rebound higher on the hard floor. We can check the prediction by measuring the first bounce on each surface.

board.text: Prediction: floor rebound is higher

text.en: Use one soft ball and a clear space away from people. Choose a release height of fifty centimetres measured from the surface underneath. Release the ball without pushing it down.

board.text: Same ball, same release height
Change only the surface

text.en: Use a paper scale fixed to the wall nearby. A partner can stand safely to one side and read the highest point of the first rebound. Agree which part of the ball you will measure.

board.text: Read the first rebound on a scale

text.en: Test both surfaces three times. Write the result from every drop in centimetres, even if two readings from the same surface do not match exactly.

board.text: Record all three trials in centimetres

text.en: Here are example readings. On the hard floor the ball rebounds thirty-one, twenty-nine and thirty centimetres. On the mat it rebounds twelve, thirteen and eleven centimetres.

board.text: Floor: 31, 29, 30 cm

text.en: All three hard-floor readings are above all three mat readings. That matches Asha’s prediction for this ball and these two surfaces.

board.text: Floor readings are higher in this test

text.en: Our conclusion applies to what we tested. Before claiming the same result for other balls or mats, we would need more evidence from those materials.

board.text: Conclusion: keep it within the evidence

text.en: Imagine one reading does not fit the others. Check whether the ball was pushed, the paper scale moved or the observer missed the top of the rebound.

board.text: Check the setup when a reading surprises you

text.en: Keep that reading in your notes. If you know why the trial was different, write that down too. Then repeat the trial with the original setup.

board.text: Keep the reading and note what happened

text.en: What if a classmate tried another ball on the mat? You could no longer tell which change caused a difference. Use the same ball on both surfaces to answer the surface question.

board.text: One question: what does the surface change?

text.en: Some questions are best answered by making careful observations. Put a short upright stick in a safe place outdoors, mark where its shadow tip falls and write down the time.

board.text: Shadow record: time, length and direction

text.en: Check it again later without moving the stick. Measure from the base to the shadow tip each time. Look at the shadow on the ground and keep your eyes away from the Sun.

board.text: Same stick and spot at every observation

text.en: Compare the marks. If you say that the shadow changed length, point to the measurements. Your record lets a classmate see how you reached that conclusion.

board.text: Use recorded lengths to support a claim

text.en: You can investigate which kind of paper soaks up more water before it wets a tray. Compare equal squares from two types of paper. Use the same dropper to make each drop about the same size.

board.text: Paper comparison: equal squares and drops

text.en: Choose what to observe before starting. You might count how many equal drops each square holds before water reaches the dry tray beneath. Use the same rule for both squares.

board.text: Choose one rule for both materials

text.en: The same way of thinking helps us in the kitchen, on a building site and when recording changes in the sky. Begin with something you can observe and use the evidence to check an idea.

board.text: Observation → question → evidence

text.en: Investigations do not always follow the same order. If a result makes you ask a better question, you may go back and plan a new comparison.

board.text: A result can lead to a new question

text.en: Think of one question from your playground. Tell a partner what you might measure, what you would keep the same, and how you would record a surprising result.

board.text: Plan a question, a fair check and a record

problem.en: How might the amount of light affect two similar seedlings over a week?

text.en: Start with two similar seedlings of the same kind. Use matching pots and soil, and give them equal amounts of water.

why.en: Start with comparable plants and keep their care alike.

text.en: Leave one seedling in light and shade the other with a cover that allows air to move. Place them nearby and check that both places stay at similar temperatures.

why.en: Try to make the amount of light the only difference.

text.en: Observe after a week and compare.

prompt.en: A friend says a plant grows taller with music. How would you check this fairly?

requiredIdeas.en: Two plants identical in every way except music.
Measure heights at the same time each day.

points.en: Steps: observe, ask, hypothesise, test, record, conclude.
A fair test changes only one thing.
Science helps us live better and needs safety and care.
